title: Navy Considers Renaming Aircraft Carrier After Trump, Replacing WWII Hero Doris Miller
excerpt: Internal discussions weigh stripping the USS Doris Miller designation from a carrier under construction and potentially honoring the sitting president instead.
body:
• The U.S. Navy is considering renaming aircraft carrier CVN-81 — currently designated USS Doris Miller — after President Donald Trump.
  • Doris Miller was the first African American awarded the Navy Cross for his heroism during the 1941 Pearl Harbor attack.
  • The carrier's keel-laying ceremony is expected by end of 2026, creating urgency around the naming decision.
  • The Navy is recommending Miller for the Medal of Honor and may name another warship after him instead.

Navy Weighs Unprecedented Renaming

The U.S. Navy is actively considering renaming an aircraft carrier under construction that was set to honor Doris Miller, a Black World War II hero lauded for his bravery during the Pearl Harbor attack, potentially switching the designation to honor President Donald Trump, according to CNN and NBC News reports published Thursday.

The Ford-class carrier, designated CVN-81, was announced as the USS Doris Miller during Trump's first term in January 2020. The naming marked the first time an aircraft carrier would honor both an enlisted sailor and an African American. But two sources familiar with internal Navy discussions told CNN there have been conversations about renaming the ship after Trump — a move that would be unprecedented, as no aircraft carrier has ever been named for a sitting president.

NBC News, citing two U.S. officials, corroborated that Navy leaders have been discussing the renaming for months.

"It's unclear what the Navy is seeking to change the name of the carrier to, though two of the sources said there have been internal conversation about renaming it to honor Trump."

— CNN, citing three sources familiar with internal discussions

Who Was Doris Miller?

Doris "Dorie" Miller was an enlisted mess attendant second class aboard the battleship USS West Virginia when Japanese bombs began falling on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. With no training on anti-aircraft weapons, Miller rushed to the smoking deck, took control of a gun, and opened fire on Japanese planes, downing at least one. He also helped carry wounded sailors, including his captain, to safety.

Miller received the Navy Cross for his extraordinary courage — the first African American to receive the honor. He was famously portrayed by Cuba Gooding Jr. in the 2001 film Pearl Harbor. Miller was later killed in action in 1943 when the escort carrier USS Liscome Bay was torpedoed in the Pacific.

The push to name a carrier after Miller spanned decades, championed by civil rights advocates and military historians who argued his heroism had been insufficiently recognized by a Navy that initially referred to him only as an "unknown Negro sailor."

Medal of Honor and a Possible Compromise

The Navy is looking to rename another warship after Miller and is recommending him for the Medal of Honor, the nation's highest military decoration, according to one source. The final authorization for the award requires congressional approval and Trump's sign-off.

Thomas Bledsoe, Miller's great-nephew, said the family had not been informed of any name change or the renewed Medal of Honor push. The family has been working to secure the Medal of Honor for Miller "for years," Bledsoe said, calling the Navy's recommendation "very positive."

The carrier is still under construction at Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia, with completion expected around 2034. But the Navy faces a time crunch: the ship's keel-laying ceremony is expected at the end of 2026, typically when names are finalized.

Broader Context

The potential renaming comes amid a series of Trump administration interventions in Navy shipbuilding. Earlier this month, Trump signed a national security memorandum directing the Navy to remove the electromagnetic aircraft launch system from CVN-81 and revert to steam catapults — a move naval experts said could cost billions and delay commissioning into the late 2030s.

A Department of Defense spokesperson said they had nothing to announce at this time.
nri_angle: The naming controversy touches on military diversity and recognition of minority heroes, issues that resonate with Indian-American service members and the diaspora.
